units.title: [IGCSE] Paper 1 Research Methods, Identity and Inequality

outcomes.text: Explain how sociologists approach studying society.
Understand the types of data and evidence used in sociology.
Understand how sociologists investigate society.
Understand positivism, including scientific methods, macro analysis, social facts, quantitative data, causation, patterns, objectivity and reliability.
Understand interpretivism, including micro analysis, meanings, motivations, qualitative data, subjectivity, validity and verstehen.
Understand approaches combining research methods and evidence, including triangulation and longitudinal studies.
Analyse and evaluate research choices using bias, interviewer effects, validity, reliability, representativeness and generalisability.
Distinguish primary, secondary, qualitative and quantitative data, and assess their respective strengths and limitations.
Understand secondary evidence sources, including statistics, documents, digital sources and media, with their strengths and limitations.
Analyse, interpret and evaluate qualitative and quantitative data using study summaries, diagrams, tables, charts and graphs.
Understand research-design stages, including topic selection, aims, hypotheses, populations, methods, operationalisation and pilot studies.
Understand sampling frames and sampling techniques, including random, systematic, stratified, snowball and quota sampling, with their limitations.
Understand surveys, questionnaires, interviews and observations, including their forms and respective strengths and limitations.
Understand open, closed, multiple-choice and scaled questions.
Understand theoretical and practical research issues, including perspectives, access, response rates, funding, cost and time.
Understand ethical issues including consent, privacy, confidentiality, deception, harm prevention and legality.
Explain how people learn their identities.
Explain how society controls people.
Explain influences on social identity.
Understand social construction through culture, norms, values, customs, roles, status and stereotypes, and its effects on behaviour and identity.
Understand the nature–nurture debate, cultural relativity, socialisation, norms and values in constructing identity.
Understand primary and secondary socialisation, its agencies and their effectiveness.
Understand socialisation processes including canalisation, hidden curricula, media representations, peer pressure, teachings, role modelling and workplace training.
Compare consensus and conflict theories of socialisation, including functionalist, Marxist and feminist explanations.

subtopics.title: Formal and Informal Control: Identity: self and society

outcomes.text: Distinguish formal and informal social control, positive and negative sanctions, and their effects on conformity.
Compare functionalist, Marxist and feminist views of social control.
Evaluate the effectiveness of government, police, courts, penal systems and armed forces as formal control agencies.
Understand formal control methods including law-making, coercion, surveillance, arrest, sentencing and imprisonment.
Evaluate family, education, peer groups, media, religion and workplaces as informal control agencies.
Understand informal control methods, including positive and negative sanctions used by families, schools, religions, workplaces and online groups.
Understand resistance through protest groups and subcultures, including reasons for joining and examples of deviant or non-conformist behaviour.
Understand how age, gender, ethnicity and social class shape individuals and groups across societies.
Evaluate how social networks, social media and virtual communities affect online identity positively and negatively.
Explain globalisation’s effects on identities, including cultural defence, hybrid identities, homogenisation, diversity, multiculturalism and global culture.
Understand postmodernist views that identity is chosen through digital identities, consumption and lifestyle choices.
Explain social stratification.
Understand stratification in open and closed societies, including status, wealth, poverty, power, mobility, meritocracy, slavery and caste.
Understand how age, gender, ethnicity and class affect life chances in education, employment, health, housing and life expectancy.
Evaluate attempts to reduce social inequalities.
Understand legislation reducing inequality through taxation, benefits, minimum wages, equal-opportunity laws and other government measures.
Explain how globalisation affects inequalities between societies.
Understand migration’s effects, including movement factors, cultural diversity, economic consequences and negative views of migrants.
Apply intersectionality to understand how age, ethnicity, gender and class combine to affect inequality.
Understand labelling and Marxist explanations of inequality, including stereotypes, master status, exploitation, ideology, poverty traps and reserve labour.
Understand how welfare states develop and affect life chances through education, benefits, pensions, housing, healthcare and basic income.
Understand how NGOs reduce global inequality through poverty reduction, medical aid, business promotion and education.
Evaluate sociological views of welfare, poverty, NGOs and equality legislation, including New Right, Marxist and feminist criticisms.
Understand how transnational companies, climate change, pollution and urbanisation affect societies.
Understand Marxist, colonial and feminist explanations of global inequality.
Explain different types of families.
Understand different family structures and evaluate their strengths and limitations.
Understand family variations and diversity across cultures, social classes and ethnic groups.
Compare New Right and postmodernist views of family diversity and assess nuclear-family dominance.
Explain the family’s role for individuals and society.
Understand functionalist views of family benefits, functions, changing functions, the warm-bath theory and nuclear-family importance.
Explain how family life is changing.
Understand demographic changes affecting families, including size, birth rates, life expectancy, ageing and later parenthood.
Understand industrialisation and urbanisation effects on family structures and roles.
Understand alternatives to family living, including single-person and shared households and friends as family.
Understand variations in marriage, including arranged, empty-shell, love, monogamous and serial-monogamous marriages.
Understand Marxist views of family support for capitalism, exploitation, class reproduction, consumption and ideological control.
Understand feminist views of patriarchy, domestic labour, abuse, conjugal roles, dual burdens, decision-making and gender socialisation.
Evaluate functionalist, Marxist and feminist explanations of the family’s role.
Assess whether family life is positive or negative for family members.
Explain changing marriage, divorce and cohabitation patterns through law, attitudes, the internet, secularisation, culture and women’s empowerment.
Understand alternatives to marriage, including cohabitation, singlehood, lone parenthood and civil partnerships.
Understand changing roles of couples, children and grandparents, including shared work, childcare, costs, support and dependence.
Understand what education and schooling mean, including their influence on individuals and society.
Compare formal and informal education, including official and hidden curricula and the behaviours and values they teach.
Understand sociological views about the roles and functions of education.
Explain and evaluate functionalist views of education, including socialisation, selection, meritocracy, mobility, role allocation and value consensus.
Understand factors explaining differences in educational achievement and experience.
Identify patterns in educational achievement and experience linked to social class, ethnicity, gender and global differences.
Assess the effectiveness, strengths and limitations of state, private, selective, single-sex, co-educational, faith and international schools.
Evaluate online learning, homeschooling, unschooling, vocational learning and progressive schooling.
Explain and evaluate Marxist views that education reproduces class inequality through capitalist control, curricula, culture, material factors and ability setting.
Explain and evaluate feminist views that education perpetuates gender inequality through patriarchy, curricula, expectations, access and peer control.
Explain class-based educational differences using material, cultural, social, linguistic, home, school and theoretical factors.
Explain ethnic differences in education using institutional racism, curriculum, role models, language, cultural factors, home influences, schools and labelling.
Explain gender differences in education using socialisation, expectations, access, cultural factors, school subcultures, labelling and feminism.
Explain international educational differences through school availability, wealth, girls’ access, class size, culture and digital resources.
Evaluate explanations for educational differences based on social class, ethnicity, gender and global variation.
Understand crime, deviance and social control, including their definitions, forms and social contexts.
Distinguish crime from deviance and explain how both vary across societies, cultures, situations and historical periods.
Understand patterns of crime and deviance and sociological explanations for them.
Identify patterns of offending and victimisation associated with age, social class, gender and ethnicity.
Understand how societies respond to crime through punishment, policing and law enforcement.
Understand punishment aims including protection, deterrence, retribution, incapacitation and rehabilitation.
Assess the effectiveness of custodial, non-custodial, financial, corporal, capital, rehabilitative and informal punishments.
Assess policing and law-enforcement strategies, including targeting, surveillance, prevention, community policing and military-style policing.

subtopics.title: Formal and Informal Control: Crime, deviance and social control

outcomes.text: Explain how formal agencies, including police, courts, government and penal institutions, control behaviour and prevent crime.
Explain how families, schools, workplaces, peers, media and religion encourage conformity and prevent crime and deviance.
Assess how effectively social-control agencies and methods promote conformity and prevent crime and deviance.
Recognise and distinguish violent, property, white-collar, expressive, instrumental, gang, green, global, cyber, hate and domestic crimes.
Compare official statistics, self-report studies and victim surveys, including their limitations and unreported or unrecorded crime.
Explain age-related crime and deviance through policing, stereotyping, self-fulfilling prophecy, gangs, socialisation, opportunity and status frustration.
Explain ethnic patterns of crime and deviance through racism, prejudice, policing, deprivation, stereotyping, gangs and status frustration.
Explain gendered crime and deviance through chivalry, masculinity, socialisation, misogyny, stereotyping, gangs and unequal opportunities.
Explain class patterns of crime and deviance through exclusion, deprivation, socialisation, opportunity, status frustration, power and policing.
Understand postmodernist, interactionist, functionalist, Marxist and feminist explanations of crime and deviance.
Evaluate explanations of crime and deviance based on age, ethnicity, gender, social class and sociological theories.
